summary: A completely passive Ethernet tap: no power, no chips, nothing for the target network to detect. You also need two capture interfaces to see both directions. If you need silent gigabit capture, this is the wrong tool - you want a proper aggregating tap or a SPAN port.

summary: A low-profile PCIe x1 FPGA card that turns any spare slot into a direct memory access port: with PCILeech you can read and write the target's RAM at over 190 MB/s without any software on the target, dump credentials, or manipulate kernel structures. honest_take: It does nothing at all against a machine with VT-d/IOMMU enabled and properly configured - which is the default on most current laptops with virtualisation-based security. It also needs physical access to an internal slot, so the threat model is 'evil maid with a screwdriver', not remote attack. And note the crowd this hardware now mostly serves: the DMA board market is driven by game cheating, which is why cards are cheap and why some vendors ship deliberately spoofed device IDs.

EMFI is also not a magic unlock button - you are searching a large parameter space for a fault that happens to land somewhere useful, and plenty of targets never yield. skill_note: The cheapest genuinely guided route into voltage glitching, because the courses come with it.
build_note: Assembled board; you supply target boards.
summary: A USD 49 voltage fault-injection board built around an RP2040 with a crowbar MOSFET, a two-channel analogue switch for voltage dipping or re-powering, 5 ns glitch resolution and an integrated SWD probe so you can glitch a chip and then dump it with the same tool. Designed as the companion hardware to Hextree's free fault-injection course material.
honest_take: It only does voltage glitching - no EM injection - so targets that need EMFI are out of scope. Practice targets ('Glitch Tags') are treated as consumables because they break, which is an ongoing cost the headline price hides. And it has been hard to buy: out of stock at the time of writing. But at USD 49 with a real course behind it, this is the least wasteful way to find out whether you actually like fault injection before spending ChipWhisperer money.
best_for: Learning voltage fault injection with structured material
Reproducing known attacks such as the nRF52 APPROTECT bypass
Cheap glitching plus SWD dumping in one board
not_for: Anyone who needs it in stock today
